# Causal Decomposition of the AIxCC Security Gap: Human vs. AI Bottleneck in Finding the Hardest Bugs

**Problem:** AIxCC reached 77% detection. The 23% gap could be caused by: (a) insufficient formal specification of the target behavior, (b) lack of deep domain knowledge (protocol-specific logic), (c) structural limitations of current LLM reasoning. These causes require different interventions.

**Direction:** Select 10 AIxCC undetected vulnerabilities from the SoK paper. For each, attempt to detect it using: (a) enhanced formal specification, (b) domain expert hint injection, (c) an LLM with extended context (full codebase). Measure which intervention closes more of the gap.

**Why it matters:** Knowing the causal structure of the 23% gap directs research toward the right intervention. If formal spec is the bottleneck, invest in better spec tools. If domain knowledge is the bottleneck, invest in specialized models.

**Relevant context:** AIxCC SoK paper (arXiv 2602.07666) analyzes undetected vulnerabilities at a structural level but does not test targeted interventions. Open-source finalist systems are being released, enabling experimentation.

title: Proof Decomposition as a Capability Scaffold: Does Breaking Proofs into Smaller Obligations Help LLMs?

original_idea.body:
# Proof Decomposition as a Capability Scaffold: Does Breaking Proofs into Smaller Obligations Help LLMs?

**Problem:** Large monolithic Lean 4 proof goals are harder than small, decomposed ones. Whether automatically decomposing proof goals into smaller sub-obligations (proof splitting) before passing to an LLM improves success rate is not tested.

**Direction:** For 30 VeriBench tasks, implement two conditions: (a) full proof goal passed to LLM, (b) goal automatically split into sub-goals (using Lean's intro, cases, constructor tactics as scaffolding), then each sub-goal passed to LLM. Compare compilation rate and total tokens used.

**Why it matters:** If decomposition improves success without additional compute, it is a free improvement to the verification pipeline. This mirrors how human Lean experts work (decompose first, prove each piece). Understanding this causal mechanism informs agent design.

**Relevant context:** Proof decomposition is standard practice in interactive theorem proving. LLM performance on smaller context problems is known to be better. Whether this transfers to formal verification is the untested causal link.

# Success State for Human-AI Collaborative Formal Verification: A Time-to-Verify Benchmark

**Problem:** Define a success state: a developer with no Lean expertise can formally verify a 50-line security-critical function in under 2 hours using AI assistance. Measure current baseline and identify the largest gap.

**Direction:** Recruit 10 CS students (no Lean experience). Each attempts to formally verify a 50-line security-critical function using available AI tools (Leanstral, Claude + VSCode Lean plugin). Measure time-to-proof, whether they succeed, and where they get stuck. Compare to the 2-hour success state.

**Why it matters:** Defining the success state in human terms (time, expertise required) makes the goal concrete and actionable. Current benchmarks measure AI capability in isolation; this measures the human-AI system's practical utility.

**Relevant context:** RAND's vision requires that formal verification become accessible to non-expert developers. No user study measures the time cost for a novice+AI to complete a real security verification task. This establishes the baseline gap.

title: Compounding Risk: AI-Generated Code × AI-Generated Tests = Correlated False Assurance

original_idea.body:
# Compounding Risk: AI-Generated Code × AI-Generated Tests = Correlated False Assurance

**Problem:** When the same or similar LLMs generate both code and tests, both may share systematic blind spots. The resulting test suite provides correlated rather than independent assurance. Combined with AI-generated formal specs (same model), all three layers of assurance are correlated.

**Direction:** Compare three conditions on 20 programs: (a) AI-generated code + AI-generated tests + AI-generated spec (same model), (b) AI code + human tests + AI spec, (c) AI code + AI tests + human spec. Inject 30 known bugs per program. Measure bug detection rate per condition. Test whether correlated assurance (condition a) is significantly worse.

**Why it matters:** Security stacks assume independent layers of assurance. If AI homogenization makes all assurance layers correlated, the stack provides the appearance of multi-layer assurance with the effective assurance of a single layer. This is a critical AI safety × formal verification compounding risk.

**Relevant context:** AI homogeneity as a systemic risk is discussed in AI safety literature. The specific compounding of correlated code+test+spec generation from the same model is not studied. This is directly relevant to vibe coding pipeline risks.
